stemBlocks.value: The function g is defined by g(x) = (x + 1)/(x − 1). (i) Calculate g(1/2). (ii) Given that g²(x) = g[g(x)], g³(x) = g[g²(x)] and so on, show that g²(x) = x and hence deduce the value of g²¹(1/2).
Think first: Once you show that applying g twice returns x, applying g twenty-one times is the same as applying it once.

stemBlocks.altText: Source visual for edmar-csec-p140-q02 from workbook page 140.

solutionSteps.instruction: Write g[g(x)] with (x + 1)/(x − 1) in place of x.

contentBlocks.value: Result: A fraction inside a fraction

solutionSteps.instruction: Combine top and bottom over the denominator x − 1.

contentBlocks.value: Every pair of applications returns to x, and 21 = 2 × 10 + 1

strategyBlocks.value: Substitute x = 1/2 to get g(1/2), then form g[g(x)] and simplify it to x; use that to reduce g²¹ to a single application of g.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (i) g(1/2) = -3  (ii) g²(x) = x, so g is self-inverse; since 21 is odd, g²¹(x) = g(x) and therefore g²¹(1/2) = -3.

whyThisWorks.value: A function satisfying g[g(x)] = x is its own inverse: it maps every value to a partner and that partner straight back again. Repeated application therefore alternates between just two states, so only whether the exponent is odd or even matters — even numbers of applications give x, odd numbers give g(x). Recognising this replaces twenty-one calculations with one.

commonErrors.misconception: Trying to evaluate g twenty-one times instead of finding the pattern.
